analysis.one_liner: Bans electric utilities from shutting off power during extreme heat or cold.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with one sponsor and nine cosponsors, never received a committee vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal utility rules so that electricity cannot be cut off during an extreme heat or extreme cold weather event. It lets state regulators or, for utilities they don't oversee, the utilities themselves decide what counts as an extreme weather event, and it requires the shutoff-protection rules to be reviewed at least once a decade. Utilities could still suspend service briefly in a specific area for safety, such as to prevent fires.
analysis.who_benefits: Households at risk of losing power over an unpaid bill during dangerous weather — especially elderly and disabled customers, low-income families, and people with medical equipment that needs electricity. Heat and cold kill Americans every year, and losing power during a heat wave or cold snap can be deadly for people without the money to pay, move, or keep a generator running.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households facing power shutoffs in extreme weather

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes into federal law that electric service may not be terminated during an extreme heat or extreme cold weather event, treating such a shutoff as especially dangerous to health.

It leaves the procedures in place that already require reasonable protections for elderly and disabled customers, and it directs state regulators or nonregulated utilities to update their shutoff procedures at least once every 10 years to reflect changing climate conditions.
It preserves a safety exception: service can still be temporarily suspended in specific areas for safe operation and maintenance of the grid, including reducing fire risk.

analysis.who_pays: Electric utilities would carry unpaid bills for customers who cannot be disconnected during extreme weather, and those costs could be spread across other customers through rates. State regulators and nonregulated utilities also take on the work of defining extreme weather events and rewriting their procedures.

drawbacks.text: Utility unpaid bills do not disappear; shutoff moratoria can push unpaid balances onto other customers through rates, and the bill includes no arrears relief or funding mechanism to cover the cost.

The bill leaves it to state regulators or, for utilities outside their jurisdiction, the utilities themselves to decide what counts as an extreme heat or cold event, so the protection is only as strong as each state's or utility's own definition.
The shutoff rules are framed as protections for customers rather than forgiveness of debt, so balances can keep accruing and be collected once the weather emergency ends.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and narrow: preventing deaths by keeping power on when heat or cold turns dangerous. The main cost is unpaid bills that get shifted to other ratepayers, which the bill does not address with funding or debt relief. The loose definition of 'extreme weather event' left to states and utilities makes the protection uneven, but the provision is modest, time-limited by weather conditions, and includes a grid-safety exception.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy subcommittee, and no markup or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Suzan DelBene introduced the bill on November 15, 2022, less than two months before the 117th Congress ended, with Rep. Lisa Blunt Rochester as the cosponsoring introducer.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on November 15, 2022, and to that committee's Subcommittee on Energy on November 16, 2022.
No further action was taken: the bill received no committee vote, no floor vote, and was not taken up by the Senate before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electric utilities and state utility regulators are better off: no new federal restriction on disconnecting customers during extreme weather was created, and utilities keep their existing ability to cut off service for nonpayment in any weather.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Utilities, which keep existing shutoff powers

for.name: Rep. Suzan DelBene
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban electric shutoffs during extreme heat and cold events and referred it to committee.

for.name: Rep. Lisa Blunt Rochester
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its second name.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; no markup was ever scheduled
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on November 15, 2022, sent it to its Energy subcommittee the next day, and never took it up for a vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters — the sponsor and nine cosponsors — were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on; no votes were ever recorded, so party split is inferred from the sponsor and cosponsor list.

industries.note: The bill would bar utilities from disconnecting customers for nonpayment during declared extreme heat or cold events, leaving them with unpaid balances and spreading those costs to other ratepayers. Utilities also gain new discretion over what counts as an extreme event where they are not state-regulated.
